title: Ὄνος ⟨παλιούρους ἐσθίων⟩ καὶ ἀλώπηξ
titleEn: The Donkey Eating Thorns and the Fox
part: The Donkey Eating Thorns and the Fox (Chambry 280 · Perry 360)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 280 (= Perry 360). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A donkey was eating the sharp mane of thorn-bushes.
sentences.i: A donkey was browsing the sharp bristling growth of thorn-bushes.
sentences.n: χαίτη is properly a horse's mane, carried over to the bristling top-growth of a shrub. ὀξείην is the Ionic form of ὀξεῖαν, and the body of this fable is verse, not prose — Chambry prints it as four short lines, its source being the verse tradition rather than the prose collection.

sentences.t:
Τὸν δ’ εἶδεν ἀλώπηξ, κερτομοῦσα δ’ εἰρήκει·
« Πῶς οὕτως ἁπαλῇ καὶ ἀνειμένῃ γλώσσῃ
σκληρὸν μαλάσσεις προσφάγημα καὶ τρώγεις ; »
sentences.tr:
Ton d’ eiden alōpēx, kertomousa d’ eirēkei·
« Pōs houtōs hapalēi kai aneimenēi glōssēi
sklēron malasseis prosphagēma kai trōgeis ; »
sentences.l: And a fox saw him, and jeering had said: « How, with a tongue so soft and so slack, do you soften a hard relish and chew it? »
sentences.i: A fox saw him and said mockingly: « How is it that with a tongue as soft and yielding as that you make a hard mouthful soft and munch it down? »
sentences.n: εἰρήκει is a pluperfect of λέγω used, as verse often uses it, for a plain past. ἀνειμένῃ is the perfect passive participle of ἀνίημι, 'let go slack'. προσφάγημα is what one eats alongside the bread — a relish; calling the thorns a relish is the fox's joke.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος πρὸς τοὺς σκληροὺς καὶ ἐπικινδύνους προφέροντας διὰ γλώσσης λόγους.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos pros tous sklērous kai epikindynous propherontas dia glōssēs logous.
sentences.l: The fable is directed at those who bring forth harsh and dangerous words by way of the tongue.
sentences.n: A closing tag with no verb: πρός with the accusative simply names the people the fable is aimed at. σκληρός is the same word used of the thorns the donkey chews, so the moral takes up the fable's own image — a soft tongue managing hard matter.
